counterexample: Could a caller retrieve another tenant's invoice? The strongest counterexample: user={'authenticated': True, 'tenant_id': 'A'} requesting invoice_id whose record has tenant_id 'B'. At service.py:4 the record is fetched, but at service.py:5 may_read returns False (security_config.py:154: 'A' != 'B'), so service.py:6 raises PermissionError and line 7 never executes. No data is returned. A second counterexample: user={'authenticated': False, 'tenant_id': 'A'} — security_config.py:152 returns False, denied. A third: user missing 'authenticated' entirely — user.get('authenticated', False) is False, denied. The only residual edge is both tenant_ids absent (None==None), which requires authenticated=True and no tenant_id on either side; the operator-supplied context supplies tenant_id, so this is not a demonstrated violation of the stated property.
assessment: The REJECTED verdict is upheld. The guard may_read is invoked on the sole retrieval path (service.py:5) and enforces both authentication (fail-closed default) and tenant equality before the data-returning sink (service.py:7). No bypass path exists across the three fully-read files. The fetch-before-check ordering does not leak because the local invoice object is only exposed via the post-guard return. The None==None tenant edge is a defense-in-depth observation, not a demonstrated violation under the operator-supplied context, and is recorded as a limitation rather than a confirmed finding.
